stem:
A 58-year-old man with longstanding hypertension starts a new oral drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. Two weeks later, laboratory studies show a rise in plasma angiotensin I with a concurrent fall in angiotensin II, and his blood pressure improves.

Which step did the drug most directly interrupt?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary ACE changing angiotensin I into II
options.misconception: None; ACE in the lungs converts inactive angiotensin I to active II.
options.explanation: ACE from the lungs converts angiotensin I to biologically active angiotensin II; blocking ACE stops that step.

options.label: B
options.text: Renin making angiotensin I from angiotensinogen
options.misconception: The upstream renin step is being confused with ACE blockade.
options.explanation: Renin still forms angiotensin I; ACE inhibition blocks the subsequent I→II conversion.

options.label: C
options.text: Adrenal making aldosterone after angiotensin II
options.misconception: A downstream steroid step is being treated as the ACE target.
options.explanation: Aldosterone synthesis is downstream of angiotensin II, not the ACE cleavage itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Liver secreting more angiotensinogen into plasma
options.misconception: Precursor production is being confused with ACE activity.
options.explanation: Angiotensinogen supply is not the ACE-catalyzed I→II conversion interrupted here.

options.label: E
options.text: Pituitary releasing ADH independent of angiotensin
options.misconception: An unrelated osmoregulatory peptide is being substituted.
options.explanation: ADH release is not the ACE step that activates angiotensin II.

context: Learning objective: infer that ACE blockade interrupts pulmonary conversion of angiotensin I to II.
